newsitem.title: IRAQ: Baghdad resumes fuel supplies to Kurdish north.
newsitem.headline: Baghdad resumes fuel supplies to Kurdish north.

text.p: Iraq, in a bid to reintegrate Iraqi Kurdistan into the national economy, has resumed fuel supplies to the Kurdish north, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported on Friday.

"In the morning today a fleet of tens of tankers headed towards the self-rule provinces to supply all filling stations with kerosene, petrol and liquified gas to meet the citizens needs of these products," INA said, quoting Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed.
The removal of curbs on fuel supplies to Iraqi Kurds follows a ruling by President Saddam Hussein on Wednesday to lift Baghdad's internal blockade on their areas, imposed in 1991.

The move is part of a package of sweeteners to strengthen the position of Massoud Barzani, the Kurdish rebel leader who last month requested Saddam's military assistance to oust a rival Kurdish group from northern Iraq.
The flow of trade and people to Kurdish provinces in the north was in full swing again, with tens of thousands of people moving in both directions, traders and travellers said.
They said Iraqi dinars, printed after the 1991 Gulf War and in circulation in government areas, were now convertible in the northern areas.
In common circulation in northern Iraq were pre-Gulf War dinars printed in Switzerland. The exchange rate, traders said, was 50 Iraqi-printed dinars to one Swiss-made dinar.

Barzani's rebels of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) are virtually in control of most of northern Iraq after routing rivals of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) headed by Jalal Talabani in less than two weeks of clashes.
U.N. relief officials in Baghdad said the flow of fuel to Iraqi Kurds was certain to alleviate sufferings resulting from acute shortages of kerosene, gas and petrol.
"There are no more trees left on mountains and hills close to Kurdish villages and towns. The Kurds felled them and used them for cooking and heating," one official said.
Diplomats in Baghdad said the move was bound to have a positive impact on the economy of Iraqi Kurdistan, crippled by U.N. trade sanctions and a sweeping internal embargo on Iraq.
Previously a litre of petrol in rebel-held areas in northern Iraq cost about 6,000 dinars, approximately $6, many times its cost in the rest of the country.
Rasheed told INA that Iraqi tankers had ferried more than 50 million litres of petrol, gas and kerosene to the citizens of Dahouk, Arbil and Sulaimaniya in the north.
In a separate report, INA said Iraqi technicians headed to northern Iraq to repair and operate filling stations there.

It said Izzat Ibrahim, vice-chairman of the Revolutionary Commmand Council (RCC), ordered Iraqi ministries to provide municipal services to Kurdish areas. It said more teams of Iraqi technicians were on their way to northern Iraq to repair water and power stations as well as communication centres.

The trade ministry, INA said, decided to include the approximately three million inhabitants of the area in the government's rationing system. It said the Kurds, who went without rations for the past six years, would receive the same amount of sugar, rice, flour, cooking oil, tea and soaps which is handed out to Iraqis in the rest of the country.
